newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Stricken Mir stable, tired crew warned of risks.
newsitem.headline: Stricken Mir stable, tired crew warned of risks.

text.p: The crippled Mir space station was stable on Friday but Mission Control warned the weary Russian-American crew they face serious risks repairing it once an unmanned supply craft arrives in about 10 days.

"For the first time, I feel that the situation on the station has stabilised," a spokeswoman at the Korolyov Mission Control near Moscow quoted commander Vasily Tsibliyev as saying two days after the worst accident of Mir's 11 years in space.

Another Russian official told reporters the cosmonauts -- Tsibliyev, flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39, and American physicist Michael Foale, 40 -- were "experiencing emotional and physical stress" and had been told to rest over the weekend.
"When do we get time to sleep?" one of the exhausted cosmonauts was heard asking mission control on Friday afternoon.

Deputy mission chief Sergei Krikalyov warned them they faced a very tough job. The Russians will have to don spacesuits and Foale will sit in the escape capsule for safety as they try to restore vital electric power supplies from the Spektr scientific module. It was holed on Wednesday during docking manoeuvres.

"Guys, it seems you will have to make a sortie to the Spektr module," reporters at Mission Control heard Krikalyov say. "And you, Mike, if this happens, will have to sit in the escape capsule." "It's very problematic," one of the Russians replied.

"It will be a very complicated operation," Russian Space Agency chief Yuri Koptev told reporters. The repair mission would require special adapters for their space suits and a special airtight door device, being manufactured this weekend.

Both pieces of equipment will be delivered along with other supplies aboard an unmanned Progress cargo craft to be launched on July 4 or, at the latest, July 5 from Russia's Baikonur cosmodrome. The trip to Mir should take about two days.

Until then, with their electricity cut by nearly a third after Spektr and its four solar panels were sealed off, there is not much the three cosmonauts can do. Many of the station's systems have been shut down, experiments are halted and they are not allowed to exert themselves to save air and power.

Mir is hotter, clammier and darker than usual, making for a long, bleak wait for help, although officials insist they are in no immediate danger and can always take to the "lifeboat" -- the three-man Soyuz TM escape module moored alongside.
Russian officials say they do not want the crew to evacuate, which could spell the end for the world's only orbital station.

"We face two tasks -- to ensure the safety of the cosmonauts and to carry out repair works to bring the flight system back to life," Yuri Semyonov, head of the Energiya space manufacturing company, said. "We are not going to abort Mir's mission."

Koptev said the next Mir crew, Anatoly Solovyov, Pavel Vinogradov and the Frenchman Leopold Eyharts, had begun training so that they could continue the repairs. They are due to leave for Mir on August 5. That timetable could change, however.

Eyharts mission is part of a European cooperation deal on Mir which, with NASA, has bankrolled the cash-strapped Russian cosmos programme since the end of the Cold War space race. Mir has been a test-bed for the international space station Alpha, the first section of which Russia is due to launch next year.

The latest accident, rated a "five" on Russia's seven-point space emergency scale, comes after a serious fire in February and a host of other mishaps and financial problems that have sparked calls in Washington for NASA to dump the Russians.

However, the head of NASA's Mir programme Frank Culbertson said it was too soon to consider the future of NASA's missions to Mir, saying an end to supply trips by the U.S. space shuttle would make it hard for the station to survive.

If Mir were abandoned, recalling memories of the nearly disastrous mission of the U.S. Apollo 13 in 1970, the world's governments would also face a 140-tonne headache. Mir could drift back toward Earth and, since it is far too big to burn up in the atmosphere, it could well fall on a built-up area.
The long wait will be a test for the crew's families.

Tsibliyev's wife Larisa told a Russian newspaper her husband's intensive survival training in extreme situations would pull him through the ordeal. And if that was not enough, he was carrying a plastic rabbit given to him by their daughter.
"It may not be pretty, but it always works," she said.

Foale, who has been on Mir since May, may have suffered most from the loss of the Spektr module. Not only has he lost his computer equipment, he has also been separated from his sleeping area -- and his toothbrush. NASA promised to send him a new one.
But Culbertson said: "Mike sounds very positive and upbeat. He sees it as a quite interesting adventure at this point."
He warned, however, that the task ahead remained risky.
"I think it is going to be a very difficult job," he told reporters in Florida. "I don't think you can take it lightly. It's going to be interesting for the world to watch this."
